svg.text: Building Multimodal Data Pipelines
Automatic Transcription, OCR & Semantic Search
DeepLearning.AI + Snowflake · Lesson 2 · multimodal building blocks
study note · v16
🎯 One-line essence
Turn audio and images into text, slice that text into small overlapping chunks, embed every chunk into
the same vector space — now one query can search across speech and slides at once.
🎬 Why this lesson? Video = audio + frames
Video is just two things glued together: a soundtrack plus a sequence of still images.
If we learn how to process audio and images on their own, we already have most of what we need to
process video. This lesson builds those two pieces with ASR for audio and OCR for images.
🎤 Audio → text (ASR)
Automatic Speech Recognition turns
spoken audio into a written transcript.
handles accents, noise, many speakers
🖼 Image → text (OCR)
Optical Character Recognition pulls
text out of slides, screenshots, scans.
handles complex layouts, tables, handwriting
🎤 ASR pipeline — raw waveform → structured text
Modern ASR is shaped like an LLM. It starts with the raw waveform, looks at its spectrogram (a visual
picture of which frequencies are present at which times), then a neural network maps those visual
patterns to small word pieces, and a language model picks the most likely word sequence.
✅ Result: structured, searchable text with timestamps and speaker labels. Once it is text, every
tool you have for text data — grep, full-text search, embeddings, LLM prompts — works on it.
In the lab: SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.AI_TRANSCRIBE(TO_FILE(audio_path)) → transcript_text + audio_duration.
🖼 OCR — text that is trapped inside images
A lot of useful text lives inside images: lecture slides, screenshots, scanned PDFs. The bytes say
“picture”, not “text”, so you cannot search them directly. OCR is the umbrella name for any
technique that turns an image into the text it contains.
📚 Traditional OCR (then)
• matches one character at a time
• uses templates of letter shapes
• needs clean, well-formatted scans
• breaks on tables, columns, photos
fragile when reality is messy
✨ Modern OCR (now)
• deep learning reads the whole image
• predicts text sequences end-to-end
• handles tables, mixed layouts, diagrams
• even reads handwriting
robust on real-world slides and scans
In the lab: AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT reads each slide JPG from the stage and writes the extracted_text column.
✂ Chunking — cut long text into bite-size pieces with overlap
Embedding models accept only a limited input window (often 512–8192 tokens). A long meeting
transcript will not fit in one piece. Chunking also makes search more precise: a short focused chunk
matches a query better than a giant blob where the relevant idea is diluted by everything else.
⚙ Fixed-size chunking with overlap
Walk through the text with a fixed window (say 500 characters). Step forward by less than the
window size so each chunk repeats the tail of the previous one. That overlap keeps sentences
from being cut in half at chunk boundaries.
long transcript text …
chunk 0 · chars 0–500
chunk 1 · chars 450–950
chunk 2 · chars 900–1400
Each new chunk starts 450 characters after the previous one, so the last 50 characters reappear at
the start of the next chunk — that is the overlap. Goal: chunks fit inside the model limit, capture a
complete thought, and never drop context at the edges.
🧮 Embeddings — one shared vector space for everything
An embedding model maps a chunk of text to a vector — a list of numbers that describes its meaning.
Similar meanings land close together in that high-dimensional space.
The key trick: if we embed audio chunks and slide chunks with the same model, they share one space.
One query → one cosine-similarity comparison → relevant pieces of BOTH modalities at once.
🎤 Audio transcript chunks
from ASR + chunking
🖼 Slide OCR text chunks
from OCR + chunking
Embedding model
snowflake-arctic-embed-m
768-dim vectors
Shared vector space
teal = audio • purple = slides
💡 Because every point lives in the same coordinate system, the distance between any two points
means the same thing — even when one came from speech and the other from a slide screenshot.
In the lab: AI_EMBED('snowflake-arctic-embed-m', chunk_text) writes a VECTOR(FLOAT, 768) column.
🔍 Cross-modal semantic search — one query, both modalities
Embed the natural-language query with the same model, then rank every chunk by cosine similarity.
A UNION across the audio chunk table and the slide OCR table merges results into one ranked list.
❓ Natural-language query
"product features about the remote control"
embed query
same arctic-embed-m
cosine similarity vs every chunk
UNION audio chunks + slide chunks
Top-ranked results (example output)

g.text: ES2008_a chunk 5 — "sell it for about 25 euro with a profit aim…"
ES2008_b chunk 3 — "budget for the remote control design…"
slide_005.jpg — "Ranking important aspects of remote control"
ES2008_c chunk 9 — "first ideas about creating a new remote…"
slide_011.jpg — "Project finance: selling price 25 euro, profit aim 50M…"

svg.text: Note: scores like 0.77–0.82 are normal; semantic match does not need the exact words to appear.
🧪 The AMI Corpus + the four Snowflake AI calls used in the lab
Dataset: a fictional product design meeting where teammates plan a new remote control. One
meeting is split into four parts (a, b, c, d). Each part has audio, slides, and multi-angle video.
~4 audio files · ~77 slide JPGs · ~24 video clips — small enough to practice, rich enough to feel real.
AI_TRANSCRIBE
audio file → transcript
+ audio_duration
AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT
image / PDF → extracted
text via modern OCR
AI_EMBED
text chunk → 768-dim
float vector
VECTOR_COSINE_SIMILARITY
two vectors → similarity
score (closer to 1 = closer)
⚡ In practice · gotchas · takeaways
✅ Same embedding model for every modality. Mixing models breaks the shared space.
✅ Chunk size is a tradeoff: too big → relevance is diluted; too small → meaning is fragmented.
✅ Keep metadata on every chunk: source file, modality, timestamp, speaker — you need it to navigate back.
⚠ Modality imbalance: if audio has 10x more chunks than slides, audio will dominate the top results.
⚠ Watch the boundaries: always use overlap when chunking, or sentences will be cut mid-thought.
✅ Same four-step recipe — extract text → chunk with overlap → embed → cosine search — works for video next.
💡 The bigger picture: any non-text data becomes usable for AI the moment you can turn it into text and embed it.
